task.name: Land project memory by the same carrier and arming as the code from the same run
task.story_text:
## Why

TheForge is configured to land stories through pull requests. Every story pull
request forge opens is immediately armed for auto-merge, so code reaches the
release branch without an operator once branch protection is satisfied. Project
memory takes the same kind of carrier into the same branch, but that one is
opened and left un-armed, and nothing merges it but a person.

The adopter repository, configured to land stories by local merge, shows the
shape this should have. There, project memory takes the direct transport and
lands alongside the merges, so memory and code arrive by the same pattern and no
memory carrier ever waits on anyone. The two repositories differ only in
configured landing behaviour, and the transport selector already handles that
difference correctly. What does not follow the configuration is the arming.

The rationale on record is that merging the memory carrier automatically would
be forge merging into a protected branch on its own authority, which the
publication path exists to stop needing. Arming a carrier is not that authority:
it delegates the decision to the branch's own requirements, and it is the same
mechanism forge already applies to every story carrier into that same branch.
The privilege the publication path removed was a direct-commit allowlist entry,
and moving memory onto its own branch removed it already.

The cost compounds quietly. A memory carrier left open across N sprints holds N
sprints of memory. It never blocks a sprint and never grows the checkout, but a
fresh clone of the base branch is missing all of it, and the operator's only
signal is a carrier sitting on the board looking like unreviewed work. The
design note that introduced this transport named a standing "memory carrier open
for N sprints" warning as its first follow-on; that warning exists only to
compensate for a carrier that should not have been waiting.

## Acceptance criteria

- Project memory reaches the base branch by the same carrier kind and the same
  arming as the code landed by that same run, under whatever landing behaviour
  is configured. Where code lands through a carrier forge arms, the memory
  carrier is armed the same way; where code lands directly, memory continues to
  land directly.
- Arming is delegated, never asserted. Memory reaches the base branch only when
  that branch's own requirements are satisfied, a base branch that refuses stays
  refused, and no path introduced here grants forge any right over the base
  branch it does not already exercise for code.
- Where arming does not take effect — unsupported by the host, disabled on the
  repository, or refused — the carrier is still published, and the recorded
  publication end state distinguishes a carrier that was armed from one that was
  not. Publication does not fail because arming did not, and it does not report
  success in a way that leaves an unarmed carrier indistinguishable from an
  armed one.
- A memory carrier that has merged is not reopened carrying content the base
  branch already holds. A memory carrier that has not merged keeps accumulating
  onto the same branch, as it does today.
- A run that produces no pending memory publishes no carrier, arms nothing, and
  changes no recorded end state.

## Example

Today, on a repository configured to land stories through pull requests:

| Carrier | Opened | Content | Gate | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Story carriers, same window | per story | reviewed source changes | green | opened, gated, merged unattended |
| Memory carrier | 2026-08-28 | 26 sprints of generated records, no source changes | green | still open, waiting on a click |

Target behaviour, same repository: the memory carrier merges once the base
branch's requirements are satisfied, exactly as those story carriers did, and
the following sprint starts its memory branch fresh from base rather than
continuing a branch that is already N sprints deep.

Target behaviour on a repository configured to land stories by local merge:
unchanged from today — memory commits alongside the merges, no carrier, nothing
to arm.

## Notes

The transport selector keys on whether a run advances the base branch from the
project-root checkout, which is the right question and is not what this changes.
The gap is entirely in what happens to the carrier once the pull-request
transport is selected.

Gate verdict was UNAVAILABLE for this HEAD, so I ran the touched suites myself: tests/test_sprint_audit_publish.py + tests/test_coord_merge_step_state.py all pass (57 passed) and ruff is clean on every touched file. Verified MEMORY_PUBLISH_CLEAN is only ever returned with pr_url=None so the early-return guard is total, staging clearing lives inside stage_and_publish_project_memory so the early return skips only the record, and the only source-side reader of the recorded state (runner.py read_audit_publish_state) treats it as an opaque informational string, so the two new state values break no consumer.

plan_review.findings:
- [P1-impl] [openai-gpt-5.6-sol-cli] The plan's first stated risk is carried on an acceptance-criterion surface. Step 4 prevents state writes for MEMORY_PUBLISH_CLEAN only in _publish_via_memory_branch, while _commit_story_run_audits in src/theforge/sprint/audit_publish.py records AUDIT_PUBLISH_CLEAN when direct transport has no pending artifacts. Thus a lands_locally=True run can still overwrite the prior publication end state, contrary to the unqualified no-pending-memory criterion.
  Suggestion: Extend the no-state-change rule and tests to the direct publication path, or obtain an explicit specification clarification limiting this acceptance criterion to memory-branch transport.
- [P1-impl] [openai-gpt-5.6-sol-cli] Step 1 moves _step_merge into pr_auto_merge.py but does not account for its dependency on completion.py's _build_exception_context. Importing that helper back from completion.py would create an avoidable coordinator module cycle.
  Suggestion: Move the exception-context dependency to a cycle-free shared module, pass it in, or retain equivalent local exception reporting in the extracted helper.
- [P1-impl] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 4's 'return on MEMORY_PUBLISH_CLEAN' has two distinct sources: the empty-staging early return (memory_publication.py:339) and the already-on-the-branch return after a worktree/commit attempt (memory_publication.py:386). The second is a resumed or repeated publish where a carrier may exist and a prior armed/unarmed state was recorded.
  Suggestion: Dev should make the no-state-change rule non-destructive for both: skipping the record (rather than writing memory_branch_clean) is correct in each case, so a previously recorded armed state is not overwritten by a run that staged nothing new.
- [P1-impl] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 1's extraction must carry _step_merge's dependencies, not just its body — it calls _build_exception_context and logs through _pr_log, and completion.py:1337 plus tests/test_coord_merge_step_state.py:13 import it by name.
  Suggestion: Move or import those helpers alongside it and keep a re-export in completion.py so the existing import site and the runner-level arming_failed plumbing (engine.py:1638/2026, story_state.py:234) stay untouched.
- [P2] [anthropic-opus-cli] Risk 3 carried in reduced form: gh pr merge --auto failures that are not matched by _AUTO_MERGE_ARMING_MARKERS (completion.py:744-751) — mergeability conflicts, gh auth/host errors — will be recorded under the same unarmed state as a genuine arming refusal.
  Suggestion: Record the raw error and the arming_failed flag from the _step_merge result in the state detail so the operator can tell a policy refusal from a host failure; this satisfies AC3 either way and needs no separate state value.
- [P2] [anthropic-opus-cli] Arming a carrier whose base-branch requirements are already satisfied causes GitHub to merge it immediately, so this path can land memory within the same run. That is the intended delegation (identical to story carriers) but it means the following run's start point flips to base mid-story-window.
  Suggestion: No plan change needed — the existing _memory_branch_start_point ancestor check already handles it; worth an assertion in Step 5 that an armed-and-merged carrier restarts from base.
